transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-06
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes (recording auto)
Attendees: Alexa Chen (Redwood AE), Jon Rivera (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (CTO, Nautilus), Liam O'Connor (Principal Eng), Sofia Reyes (DevOps), Evan Brooks (Product), Zara Khan (Security)

Summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Nautilus is evaluating Redwood for shopping-assistant and search rerank inference. Primary questions: SDKs and first-party integrations with LangChain/LlamaIndex, architecture for gateway/proxy + network egress, quotas/rate-limiting and bursting, observability hooks (per-route latency/cost), and security (KMS, audit logs, VPC). They're leaning Dedicated for predictable latency but want Hosted for faster POC. Next step: send pricing and example integrations; schedule SE-led benchmark.

Topics: SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex integration, gateway/proxy patterns, rate limits/quotas, observability hooks, Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs, security (KMS, audit logs, SSO)

Transcript:
[00:00] Alexa Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm alexa from redwood, i think we have like an hour so we'll run through integration questions, jon will cover the deep part of the architecture, i'll handle product/pricing and next steps. how's that sound?
[00:12] Maya Patel: yep good, thanks alexa. thanks for fitting us in. i'm maya, cto at nautilus, liam is our lead on infra, zara sec ops, sofia runs our platform, evan product.
[00:21] Alexa Chen: awesome, before we jump in quick one: who owns the POC success criteria? is it evan/product or maya infra-level p95 latency?
[00:30] Evan Brooks: product will own the feature success (relevance uplift + clickthrough) but infra cares about latency and cost, ideally sub-200ms p95 for live chat & sub-500ms for batch rerank.
[00:42] Liam O'Connor: and our traffic pattern is spiky - holiday peaks, but normal daily is ~150 qps, peak burst to ~1.2k qps for short windows. we need predictable scaling and cost controls.
[00:54] Jon Rivera: ok noted. quick opener: are you targeting hosted/redwood hosted for POC or Dedicated/Private?
[01:02] Maya Patel: we wanted to see Hosted for speed of setup, but we're also evaluating Dedicated because we have p95 and data residency needs. curious how easy it is to switch from Hosted to Dedicated later.
[01:15] Alexa Chen: good question. customers typically start on Hosted for quick proofs, then move to Dedicated when they need predictable throughput and private networking. switching is supported - models/versions can be pinned and the same API surface remains. jon: can you explain the typical integration patterns we see?
[01:31] Jon Rivera: yeah. three common patterns: direct SDK calls from backend -> Redwood Hosted API; a gateway/proxy in front (our recommended for multi-tenant routing, rate limiting, auth); or Private deployment where requests stay within customer VPC and we integrate with customer's load balancer. for LangChain or LlamaIndex we typically see the app run index and orchestration in customer infra and call Redwood for completions/embeddings.
[01:55] Liam O'Connor: for LangChain we use the chain-of-thought prompt and we also persist embeddings in our own vector DB. how does Redwood's SDK play with LlamaIndex? any official support?
[02:08] Jon Rivera: there's a short answer: yes. we have SDK snippets and example repos that show LangChain and LlamaIndex adapters - we also have an official helper for streaming responses so you can stream tokens into your UI. i'll drop the repo link after. note that some names in the autogen docs say Redwoo - ignore that it's a minor typo in the doc export sometimes.
[02:28] Sofia Reyes: on the gateway, curious about rate-limiting - can we set per-route quotas or per-tenant budgets? we want to avoid noisy neighbor cost spikes.
[02:37] Alexa Chen: yes, Redwood supports per-route policies and quotas. in Hosted we can apply token-based quotas and throttles per API key or per route; Dedicated gives finer policies at the pool level and you can set burst windows. we also do token-level billing so you can track cost per route.
[02:54] Zara Khan: audit logs and KMS - if we go Dedicated or Private we need HSM/KMS integration with AWS KMS, and audit logs stored for 12 months. is that supported?
[03:04] Jon Rivera: Dedicated and Private support customer-managed KMS; HSM integrations are available as an add-on. audit logs are shipped to your S3 or our telemetry pipeline depending on deployment, and retention can be configured. we'll share the security pack with exact controls.
[03:18] Maya Patel: about network architecture - if we put a small gateway/proxy in our VPC, does that add latency? we need to budget for extra roundtrips.
[03:27] Jon Rivera: minimal. recommended pattern is an edge gateway that handles auth, routing, and retry logic - p95 adds ~10-20ms depending on placement. the main contributor to latency is model choice and sequence length. we can show kernel profiles for different models.
[03:40] Evan Brooks: can we do local caching of prefix prompts or KV cache? like for session state we want minimal recompute.
[03:47] Jon Rivera: yes - Redwood runtime supports prefix/KV caching. for user sessions we often recommend using session keys and cache warmers. that's especially effective for chat-heavy workloads.
[03:55] Liam O'Connor: if we use LangChain with LlamaIndex, is there a recommended pattern to avoid double-tokenization or mismatched encoders? we've hit that with other providers.
[04:05] Jon Rivera: good point. our SDK exposes tokenizer utilities and we document best practice: use the SDK tokenizer for prompt precompute or the same encoding as your vector DB. LlamaIndex adapters in our example repo include tokenization helpers.
[04:18] Alexa Chen: the team asked about observability - does Redwood provide per-route dashboards and tracing hooks we can integrate into our Grafana?
[04:27] Jon Rivera: yes: per-route latency and cost breakdowns, token-level cost, and sampling traces. we provide a webhook and a prometheus exporter for key metrics; customers often pipe traces into Grafana/Tempo. we also have route-level SLO configs and alerts.
[04:39] Sofia Reyes: for sampling traces is the payload sanitized? we handle PII carefully.
[04:44] Jon Rivera: telemetry can be redacted before export; you can configure retention and field-level redaction. we'll include the doc with exact controls.
[04:53] Maya Patel: about quotas again - if we want a hard cap on monthly tokens per team, can that be enforced to prevent runaway costs?
[05:00] Alexa Chen: yes, you can set hard caps and soft alerts. Hosted supports quota enforcement per API key; Dedicated adds org-level policy enforcement with notifications and automatic throttling.
[05:10] Evan Brooks: what's the SDK language support? we use node + python.
[05:14] Jon Rivera: official SDKs for Python, Node, and Go - plus REST. community integrations for Java and Ruby exist. we also have LangChain connectors and LlamaIndex adapters for Python.
[05:25] Liam O'Connor: for the Dedicated pool sizing - given our baseline 150 qps and 1.2k burst, any rough guidance on GPU types?
[05:34] Jon Rivera: rough back-of-envelope: for small generation models N=8b quantized, a few A10/GPU instances could handle steady 150 qps with good batching; for 1.2k burst you'll want autoscaling with backups, or reserve burst capacity. if you need strict p95 SLAs, we'd recommend higher-memory GPUs and pinning model variants. we'll run a sizing exercise in the SE deep-dive.
[05:54] Zara Khan: compliance - do you have SOC2 reports and what about regional data residency?
[05:59] Alexa Chen: yes SOC2; we can provide SOC2 and ISO docs. for data residency Hosted has region options; Dedicated/Private gives complete control. we'll attach the compliance pack.
[06:08] Maya Patel: any pitfalls customers hit when migrating from Hosted to Dedicated?
[06:12] Jon Rivera: mostly around capacity planning and model variants; also ensuring networking (VPC peering, routing) is set up. we run a migration checklist and a staged canary deploy to verify.
[06:22] Evan Brooks: about function/tool calling and structured output - our use case requires JSON LLM outputs we can validate.
[06:29] Jon Rivera: Redwood supports structured tool-calling, function calling and schema enforcement. there's also an option to run a deterministic post-processor or schema validator in the gateway to reject non-conforming outputs.
[06:41] Sophia / Sofia (crowd noise, slight cross-talk)
[06:45] Sofia Reyes: quick Q, rate limits: do you support leaky-bucket vs fixed-window? we have per-customer SLAs so granularity is important.
[06:53] Jon Rivera: both patterns - we support leaky-bucket/rolling window and token-based rate limiting. you can define rules per API key and per route.
[07:02] Liam O'Connor: network egress charges - when using Hosted, do we pay your network egress?
[07:07] Alexa Chen: in Hosted, outbound traffic is part of pricing but large egress for private connections may be separately negotiated; for Dedicated/Private it's typically handled at the infra layer and you'll incur cloud egress based on your provider. we'll include an egress note in the pricing sheet.
[07:19] Evan Brooks: okay let's talk about instantiating embeddings via LlamaIndex - we keep vector DB in-house and only send embeddings. is batching supported?
[07:27] Jon Rivera: yes embeddings batching is recommended; the SDK supports batch endpoints and auto-batching. also you can do async calls for large uploads.
[07:35] Maya Patel: curious on token accounting accuracy - some vendors get off-by-one with streaming tokens and cost visibility.
[07:41] Jon Rivera: we expose token accounting at the shard/route level; streaming tokens are counted as emitted tokens. we can share sample token logs.
[07:50] Alexa Chen: quick pause - jon, can you demo or show code snippet for LangChain + Redwood?
[07:55] Jon Rivera: i'll paste after the call but here's the gist: from redwood import Redwood; client = Redwood(api_key=...) ; then in LangChain you use the RedwoodLLM wrapper, for LlamaIndex our adapter maps embeddings functions to redwood.embeddings.batch(). i'll include repo link, note there was a typo in README 'Redwood Dedicated' -> 'Redwood Dedicate' in one commit.
[08:20] Maya Patel: good. on authentication patterns - do you prefer API keys per service or use mTLS between our gateway and Redwood?
[08:27] Jon Rivera: both supported. Hosted typically uses API keys; Dedicated/Private supports mTLS and private endpoints. you can also front it with your own gateway and handle auth there.
[08:37] Zara Khan: SSO? we need SCIM user provisioning and RBAC.
[08:41] Alexa Chen: yes SCIM and SSO (SAML/OIDC) are supported for console access; RBAC can be mapped to teams and routes.
[08:50] Liam O'Connor: about latency budget again - you said switching models can fallback to cheaper variants - how seamless is that?
[08:58] Jon Rivera: smart routing allows fallbacks by model family; you can define fallback policies (latency-first, cost-first). when a primary model is overloaded we route to compatible variant, tokenization/response shape is preserved in most common patterns.
[09:15] Evan Brooks: do you support structured experiments / A/B at inference layer?
[09:20] Jon Rivera: yes rollouts and A/B tests are built into Redwood Console; you can do traffic splits, per-route metrics and automatic rollback.
[09:27] Maya Patel: our security team will want to run a penetration test on the gateway integration - acceptable?
[09:32] Alexa Chen: yes, we provide a test window and coordinate with our security team. we'll also provide a contact for the security review.
[09:38] Sofia Reyes: one more practical: how does rate-limiting interact with batching? if you batch many small requests for cost efficiency will rate-limiters see the aggregated token usage?
[09:50] Jon Rivera: rate-limits are token-aware; batching counts the tokens of batched request. we have controls to prefer batching but enforce per-tenant quotas. recommended approach: gateway does local batching up to a threshold, Redwood runtime does continuous batching to improve throughput.
[10:08] Evan Brooks: what about cold-starts from cache miss - is there a warm-up strategy?
[10:13] Jon Rivera: yes cache warmers and pre-initialized KV caches. for chat sessions we recommend sticky routing to preserve warmed KV cache.
[10:22] Maya Patel: how long do sessions live in KV cache?
[10:25] Jon Rivera: configurable - typically a few minutes by default, longer for stateful chat. depends on memory budgets.
[10:32] Alexa Chen: switching gears, any blockers from your side to start pilot?
[10:37] Liam O'Connor: we need security docs, pricing, and a short SE benchmark to validate p95. also want a plan for traffic shaping during holiday spikes.
[10:46] Alexa Chen: that aligns with our next steps. we'll send security/compliance pack and pricing. jon will run bench and provide model sizing.
[10:54] Maya Patel: timeline - target POC kickoff mid-may, evaluation for Dedicated by late june.
[10:59] Alexa Chen: sounds good - we'll follow up on dates.
[11:05] Evan Brooks: thank you. any notes for the LangChain integration around streaming?
[11:10] Jon Rivera: you'll want to use our streaming client with event-driven tokens; also ensure your UI handles partial objects if you stream structured JSON. we'll include examples.
[11:22] Sofia Reyes: small nit: we use Hashicorp Vault for secrets, any autointegration?
[11:26] Jon Rivera: yes we have examples for Vault and AWS Secrets Manager.
[11:31] Zara Khan: last question: if something goes wrong in the Dedicated pool who owns incident response?
[11:36] Alexa Chen: with Dedicated we have an SLA and on-call support; incident response is collaborative. for Private deployments it's customer-managed with Redwood support optionally.
[11:46] Maya Patel: ok thanks everyone, useful session. we'll review and pick dates for the SE bench.
[11:52] Alexa Chen: thanks all. jon and i will send the repo and docs. next steps recap: send pricing + security pack, LangChain/LlamaIndex examples, schedule SE bench.
[11:59] (call end)
